children.text: protkaṇṭhayanti na mano bhuvi kasya yūnaḥ

children.translated_text: Making the trees, bowed with blossoms, dance,
shaking the lotus pond with its fully-bloomed lotuses,
the wind forcibly agitates the minds of women.
Adorned with pairs of intoxicated swans,
decorated with clear, fully-bloomed lotuses and water-lilies,
with garlands of waves raised by the gentle morning breeze —
the lakes suddenly make the heart eager.
The bow of <s>Indra</s> (the rainbow) has vanished into the bellies of clouds,
lightning no longer flashes — that sky-banner;
cranes no longer fan the sky with the wind of their wings;
peacocks no longer gaze at the heavens with upraised faces.
<s>Madana</s> (Cupid), leaving the peacocks bereft of their dance performances,
now attends the swans with their sweet singing;
leaving <s>kadamba</s>, <s>kuṭaja</s>, <s>arjuna</s>, and <s>sarjanīpa</s> trees,
the beauty of blossom-emergence has approached the <s>saptacchada</s> trees.
The groves — enchanting with the fragrance of <s>śephālikā</s> flowers,
resounding with flocks of birds resting peacefully,
with blue lotuses [resembling] the eyes of deer standing at the edges —
make the minds of men yearn.
The wind at dawn, repeatedly shaking <s>kahlāra</s> lotuses, day-lotuses, and night-lilies,
having attained an even greater coolness from contact with them,
makes [people] yearn exceedingly,
while scattering the dew-drops clinging to the tips of leaves.
The borderlands — their grounds covered with abundant ripened rice,
adorned with prosperous herds of cattle resting peacefully,
resounding with flocks of swans and <s>sārasa</s> cranes —
generate delight in people.
The graceful gait of women is surpassed by swans,
the moon-like radiance of their faces by blooming lotuses,
their intoxicating eyes by blue water-lilies,
and their lovely brow-play by slender waves.
The dark creepers, with new shoots bent under the weight of flowers,
steal the beauty of women's arms adorned with ornaments;
and the fresh <s>mālatī</s> (jasmine), beautiful with <s>kaṅkelī</s> blossoms,
[steals] the moon-like radiance of their clear, tooth-revealing smiles.
Women fill their hair — dense, dark, with curled tips pulled tight —
with fresh <s>mālatī</s> (jasmine) flowers,
and in their ears, alongside excellent golden earrings,
they place various blue lotuses.
With necklaces mixed with sandal-paste, [they adorn] the circles of their breasts;
with girdle-strings, their ample hips;
with tinkling anklets, their lotus-feet —
women, their minds delighted, adorn themselves today.
Of the lakes — strewn with blooming white water-lilies, frequented by royal swans,
beautified by water gleaming like emerald gems —
the heavens, free of clouds, strewn with moon and stars,
bear a beauty of surpassing loveliness [rivaling those lakes].
In autumn, the winds blow cool from contact with <s>kumuda</s> (night-lilies);
the quarters of the sky, free of cloud-masses, are charming;
the water is free of murkiness, the earth [free] of thick mud;
the sky [shines] with a moon of pure rays, variegated with stars.
Some young women — their hands lovely as lotuses, clasped with their lovers' —
their faces outshining the moon,
generally proceed to their homes, made fragrant with flowers,
having abandoned the melody of song due to the force of powerful desire.
Possessed of the grace of love's delight, gathered with their good companions,
they abundantly suggest the sport of the Unequal-arrowed One (<s>Anāṅga</s>, Cupid);
with incomparable lip-color, in the middle of the night,
young women with fresh lovers display their pleasures in autumn.
Pressed by the sun's rays at dawn,
the lotus — resembling a fair young woman's face — opens today;
and the night-lily, when the moon's orb has set, closes —
like the smile of brides whose beloveds are away.
Recognizing the beauty of his beloved's dark eyes in the blue lotuses,
the tinkling of her golden girdle in the calls of the intoxicated swans,
the lovely splendor of her lips in the <s>bandhujīva</s> flower,
the traveler now weeps, his mind bewildered.
Leaving the moon-like radiance in women's faces,
the desirable sound of swans in jeweled anklets,
the <s>bandhūka</s> radiance in charming lips —
the fortunate beauty of autumn's arrival departs to some [unknown] place.
With a face of blooming lotuses, eyes of full-blown blue water-lilies,
wearing garments white as blossomed fresh <s>kāśa</s>-grass,
with the charming radiance of night-lilies — like an intoxicated woman of desire —
may this autumn bestow the highest delight upon your hearts!
Fourth Canto.
Lovely with the emergence of new shoots and crops,
with <s>lodhra</s> trees in bloom, with ripened rice,
with lotuses vanished, with frost beginning to fall —
this early winter season (<s>hemanta</s>) has arrived.
With charming necklaces — white as sandal-paste,
as frost, <s>kunda</s> (jasmine), and the moon —
the circles of breasts of buxom women of pleasure
are no longer adorned [with such cool ornaments].
On the paired arms of women of pleasure,
bracelets and arm-bands no longer find a place;
nor fresh silk garments on the orbs of their hips,
nor thin fabrics on their full bosoms.
Women do not adorn their hips
with girdle-strings studded with variegated gold and gems,
nor their lotus-feet — possessing the beauty of lotuses —
with anklets that echo the sound of swans.
Women anoint their limbs with <s>kālīyaka</s> (black aloe),
their lotus-faces with decorative leaf-patterns,
their heads with the fragrance of dark aloe-wood incense —
for the festival of love-making.
Young women — their faces pale and wan from the exhaustion of love-sport,
having attained the arising of delight —
do not laugh aloud, [but rather] gaze at
their lips, bitten by teeth-tips and pressed [during passion].
Having encountered the beauty of women's full breasts and chests,
worn out from pressing against them,
the cold season, with frost drops clinging to grass-tips, falling,
cries out, as it were, at dawn.
The borderlands — strewn with abundant crops of rice,
adorned with herds of doe-eyed deer,
resounding enchantingly with the cries of <s>krauñca</s> (curlew) birds —
make the heart eager.
The lakes — adorned with blooming blue water-lilies,
decorated with intoxicated <s>kādamba</s> (geese),
with clear, delightfully cool water —
steal the hearts of men.
Seeing the road thoroughly drained of water,
[wives] bearing their husbands weary from travel,
gazed upon [longingly] by doe-eyed women,
seem to awaken [their] desires.
Ripening, constantly shaken
by winds made cold by frost,
the <s>priyangu</s> (millet) creeper, separated from her beloved,
turns pale, like a woman of pleasure.
With faces fragrant with the scent of flower-wine,
bodies perfumed by the warmth of [each other's] breath,
lying in mutual bodily embrace,
people sleep, pierced by the nectar of desire.
By their lips bearing the wounds and tooth-marks,
and breasts inscribed by fingertip scratches,
the merciless love-enjoyment of young women
in the bloom of youth is revealed.
One woman, mirror in hand, adorns
her lotus-face in the morning sunlight,
and pulling down her lip — whose essence was drunk by her lover,
bitten by his teeth-tips — she examines it.
Another, her body wearied by the exertion of abundant love-play,
her lotus-eyes reddened from the night's wakefulness,
her mass of hair disheveled and loosely falling from her drooping shoulders,
falls asleep, warmed by the gentle rays of the sun.
Removing from their heads the wilted garlands whose lovely fragrance has been enjoyed,
[they] with dense, dark tresses
and bodily grace bowed by the weight of full, uplifted breasts,
other young women arrange their hair.
Another, seeing her body enjoyed by her lover,
joyful, her lips arranged in beautiful radiance,
puts on her bodice, her limbs marked by nail-scratches,
with dangling dark, lovely curled locks, her eyes half-closed.
Others, having reached exhaustion from prolonged exertion
in the sport of love-play, their bodily grace relaxed,
the tips of their breasts bristling with horripilation,
beautiful women apply their unguents.
Charming in many ways, stealing the hearts of women,
with village borders busy with abundant ripened rice,
with frost falling, sung by the cries of <s>krauñca</s> birds —

children.text: pradiśatu himayuktaḥ kāla eṣaḥ sukhaṃ vaḥ
children.translated_text: may this frost-laden season bestow happiness upon you!
Fifth Canto.
The earth covered with grown rice and sugarcane fields,
made lovely here and there by the resounding cries of <s>krauñca</s> birds,
fully satisfying desire, dear to women —
hear, O beautiful-thighed one, of the season called <s>śiśira</s> (winter)!
The interiors of mansions with windows shut against the wind,
the fire, the rays of the sun,
heavy garments, young women in their prime —
these become the objects of people's service in this season.
Neither sandal-paste cool as moonbeams,
nor the terrace of a mansion pure as the autumn moon,
nor winds cold with dense frost
delight the hearts of people now.
Cold from the onslaught of masses of frost,
further chilled by the moon's rays,
adorned beautifully with clusters of pale stars —
the nights are not fit to be endured by people.
Having taken betel, unguents, and garlands,
their lotus-faces scented with flower-wine,
abundantly perfumed with the incense of dark aloe-wood —
women eagerly enter the bedchamber.
Seeing their husbands — who had committed offenses, threatened many times,
trembling, their minds robbed by apprehension —
now desirous of love-making,
the women joyfully forgot those offenses.
By youths fully desirous, mercilessly,
during the long nights, enjoyed for a long time,
their breasts moving slowly from the fatigue and weariness,
young women in the bloom of youth wander languidly at night's end.
With breasts compressed by lovely bodices,
their chests adorned with colored silken garments,
their hair set with flowers within —
women seem to adorn the winter season itself.
With breasts golden-tawny from saffron (<s>kuṅkuma</s>) paste,
pleasantly warm with the heat of fresh youth,
pressed to the chests of women of pleasure,
lovers sleep, conquering the cold.
With blue lotuses trembling from fragrant sighs,
enchanting, awakening the desire for love,
at night, delighted women, together with their lovers,
drink the finest wine, intoxicating.
One woman at dawn, her intoxicated flush of passion gone,
her breast-tips pressed tight by her husband's embrace,
gazing at her body enjoyed by her dearest lover,
goes from her sleeping garment to another dress, laughing.
Another woman of desire, bearing her mass of hair
fragrant with incense of aloe-wood, its flower-garland fallen, its tips curled,
with heavy hips, deep navel, slender waist —
leaves her bed at dawn, [displaying] beautiful radiance.
With face-orbs having lips beautifully copper-red, like golden lotuses,
with reddish outer corners of their eyes resting against their temples,
with hair clinging to their shoulders at dawn —
women stand within the house today like [embodiments of] <s>Śrī</s> (the goddess of beauty).
Burdened by the weight of their broad hips, slightly stooped at the waist,
walking slowly, slowly, from the weariness of their breast-weight,
swiftly discarding the attire of the nighttime love-encounter,
other young women don the dress suitable for daytime.
Gazing at the tips of their breasts marked with nail-scratches,
touching their lip-shoots bitten by teeth,
these young women delight in the memory of beloved love-play
and adorn their faces at the time of sunrise.
Abundant with preparations of jaggery, delightful with sweet rice and sugarcane,
with vigorous sports of love-play arousing the pride of <s>Kandarpa</s> (Cupid),
a cause of heart-burning for those separated from their dear ones —
may this winter season always be for your welfare!
Sixth Canto [Description of Spring].
With sharp arrows of full-blown mango shoots,
with a bowstring splendid with garlands of bees,
to pierce the minds of those given to love-play —
the warrior Spring has arrived, O beloved!
Trees are in flower, water is with lotuses,
women are with desire, the wind is fragrant,
evenings are pleasant, and days are delightful —
everything is most charming in spring, O beloved!
With mansions made cool by a slight frost,
and lovely heads perfumed with <s>campaka</s> flowers,
in the spring season women adorn
their breasts with necklaces and enchanting blossoms.
Upon the waters of ponds, upon jeweled girdles,
upon the radiance of the moon, upon women,
upon mango trees laden with blossoms —
spring bestows good fortune.
With silken garments reddened by <s>kusumbha</s> (safflower) dye,
the orbs of women's hips [are adorned];
with thin fabrics whitened by saffron (<s>kuṅkuma</s>) paste,
the circles of their breasts are decorated.
In their ears, the fitting fresh <s>karṇikāra</s> [flower],
in their waving dark locks, the <s>aśoka</s>,
and the full-blown flower of fresh <s>mallikā</s> (jasmine) —
these enhance the beauty of women.
Upon their breasts, necklaces moist with white sandal-paste;
upon their arms, bracelets and armlets find their place;
upon the hips of full-hipped women
whose minds are troubled by <s>Anaṅga</s> (Cupid) — girdles.
Upon the faces of women of pleasure —
adorned with decorative leaf-patterns, resembling golden lotuses —
the arrival of perspiration, charming with pearls between gems,
attains profusion.
Loosening the slack bindings of
their limbs agitated by <s>Kandarpa</s> (Cupid),
when their beloveds are nearby,
women become utterly eager.
Thin, pale, languid with intoxication,
constantly inclined to yawning,
<s>Anaṅga</s> (Cupid) renders the limbs of women
filled with the excitement of loveliness.
People desire the shade of trees,
and at night they wish for the moon's rays;
they go to the pleasant, cool terrace to sleep
and tightly embrace their beloved for coolness.
In the eyes — restless, in the intoxicated, languid [eyes];
in the cheeks — pale; in the breasts — firm;
in the waist — hollow; in the hips — full —
today <s>Anaṅga</s> (Cupid) dwells in manifold ways in women.
Limbs playful with the grace of drowsiness,
words somewhat languid with wine,
sidelong glances cast with a play of brows —
<s>Kāma</s> (desire) has fashioned these in the women.
Mixed with <s>priyangu</s>, <s>kālīyaka</s> (black aloe), and <s>kuṅkuma</s> (saffron),
upon their fair breasts, by women of pleasure,
sandal-paste is applied by the women
